title: Build the round-trip property suite and the 30-rule corpus gate
body:
## Context
R3 exit criterion 5 is a hard gate: "a corpus of >=30 rules authored in the form editor opens in the node editor and returns to the form editor with an identical IR (byte-equal serialisation) and vice versa." US-RULE-001's NFR sets the automated companion: "property-based tests (>=10 000 generated documents per CI run) assert round-trip equality across form→IR→node→IR→form". US-RULE-006's NFR makes the whole equivalence release-blocking: "the round-trip property test plus an E2E switch test for every construct in the metric/action vocabulary must be green before any rule feature ships."

This ticket owns that machinery. It is deliberately a QA-owned deliverable rather than a side effect of E35-T04, because the suite must be adversarial toward the implementation rather than shaped by it.

## Scope / Deliverables
- A **property-based round-trip suite** (Hypothesis) generating valid IR documents against the JSON Schema bounds and asserting, for each:
  - `hash(ir) == hash(compile_graph(to_graph_model(ir)))`
  - for form-compatible documents, `hash(ir) == hash(compile_form(to_form_model(ir)))`
  - the full hop chain from US-RULE-001's fuzz scenario: IR → node → IR → form → IR, hash unchanged at every hop, with any hop that cannot represent the document **failing loudly rather than emitting a lossy document**
  - the `presentation` block survives untouched across hops
  - >=10 000 documents per CI run, with a deterministic seed recorded per run and a shrinking configuration that produces a minimal reproducer inside 60 s.
- The **>=30-rule corpus**: hand-authored, semantically meaningful rules covering every construct in the vocabulary — all 13 triggers, every comparison operator, all four boolean ops including `n_of`, all four temporal ops, nested arithmetic, shared sub-expressions, every one of the 25 action types at least once, all five scope levels, and the eight built-in system rules. Each corpus entry carries its expected canonical hash as a golden file.
- A **golden-hash regression gate**: any change to canonicalisation, the models or the compilers that alters a corpus hash fails CI and requires an explicit, reviewed golden update with a stated reason — this is what stops a silent semantic drift.
- **Mutation sanity check**: a CI job that injects a known canonicalisation defect and asserts the suite catches it, so a suite that has quietly stopped asserting anything is detected.
- Wiring: the property suite and corpus gate are **required checks** on the merge queue for any PR touching the IR, compiler or canonicalisation packages.

## Out of scope
- The E2E editor-switch test through the real UI — **E35-Q03** (this ticket covers the compiler level).
- The editors themselves — E36/E37, which consume this suite as their regression gate.
- Performance of canonicalisation — **E35-Q04**.

## Acceptance criteria
```gherkin
Scenario: Ten thousand generated documents round-trip
  Given the property suite configured for at least 10 000 documents
  When CI runs it
  Then every document's canonical hash is unchanged across the full IR to node to IR to form to IR chain

Scenario: The thirty-rule corpus is hash-stable both directions
  Given the corpus of at least 30 hand-authored rules
  When each is taken form to graph to form and graph to form to graph
  Then the canonical hash matches its golden value in every case

Scenario: A lossy hop fails loudly (failure case)
  Given a document containing a construct the form editor cannot represent
  When the form hop is attempted
  Then it raises a named unrepresentable error rather than emitting a document with the construct dropped

Scenario: A canonicalisation defect is caught (failure case)
  Given the mutation job injecting an unsorted-keys defect
  When the property suite runs
  Then it fails and shrinks to a minimal reproducing document within 60 seconds

Scenario: Golden drift requires a human decision (edge case)
  Given a change that alters a corpus rule's canonical hash
  When CI runs
  Then the corpus gate fails, and merging requires an explicit golden update with a written reason in the PR
```

## Technical notes / design
The generator strategy comes from ADR-0016 (E35-K01) and must produce documents that are *valid*, not merely well-typed — generating semantically absurd but schema-valid rules is fine and desirable, but generating schema-invalid ones only tests the validator, which is a different suite.

Bias the generator deliberately toward the constructs where round-tripping is hard: shared sub-expressions, `n_of`, deeply nested booleans at the 32-child bound, temporal nodes wrapping boolean nodes, and arithmetic nested inside arithmetic. Uniform random generation would spend most of its budget on trivial two-condition rules.

Record the Hypothesis database in CI so a failure found once is replayed on every subsequent run — otherwise a rare failure is found, fixed by accident, and never re-verified.

Corpus authorship note: the 30 rules must be *meaningful*, because they are also the golden action-plan fixtures used elsewhere and the examples in the documentation. Derive them from the built-in system rules, the templates gallery (SCR-083) content, and the worked examples in ADR-0007 (break-even after 1R, ATR trailing, cancel-if-spread-too-wide, daily-loss lockout).

## Test plan
This ticket *is* test code. Its own correctness is established by the mutation sanity check (fourth acceptance scenario) plus review by the second QA/SDET and the backend lead. Suite runtime must fit the CI budget — target under 4 minutes for 10 000 documents, achieved by parallel workers if needed.

## Security notes
The round-trip guarantee is a safety property, not only a usability one: a lossy round trip could silently change what an armed rule does. Making these required merge checks is therefore a security control. The corpus must contain no real account ids, symbols beyond the public perpetuals, or credentials.

## Accessibility notes
N/A — test infrastructure.

## Performance notes
Suite runtime budget under 4 minutes in CI for the 10 000-document run; the corpus gate under 30 seconds. If the budget is exceeded, reduce per-document work rather than document count — the count is an NFR.

## Observability
CI reports the number of documents generated, the seed, and the shrink time on failure, so a flaky failure is diagnosable rather than mysterious. `rule_roundtrip_mismatch_total` is the production counterpart and is alerted on.

## Definition of Done
- [ ] Test artefacts committed to the repository (plan document, suites, fixtures, scripts) and runnable by any engineer from a documented command.
- [ ] Results recorded on the ticket with pass/fail per scenario and links to CI runs.
- [ ] Any defect found is filed as a Bug with reproduction steps, expected vs actual, severity, and the test layer that should have caught it earlier.
- [ ] New automated suites wired into CI with their runtime budget agreed, and marked required where the roadmap's quality gates demand it.
- [ ] Reviewed by the second QA/SDET and by the rule-engine backend lead.
- [ ] Sign-off comment posted; no P0/P1 defects open against the covered scope.
- [ ] The property suite and corpus gate are configured as **required checks** on the merge queue for PRs touching the IR, compiler or canonicalisation packages.

Blocked by **E35-Q01** (the plan defines coverage) and **E35-T04** (there must be compilers to round-trip through). Its corpus is consumed by **E35-Q03**, **E36** and **E37**; the suite gates all three.

title: Build the determinism suite and the rule-engine end-to-end tests
body:
## Context
Two gates converge in this ticket. R3 exit criterion 6: "Rule runtime is deterministic over replay: the same recorded window produces the same action sequence across runs." And the R3 E2E quality gate: "Playwright web + Electron covering ticket, chart trading, DOM trading, bracket, fan-out, **rule creation in both editors**, alert firing, journal capture."

Determinism is the property that makes everything else in this epic testable — if the same input can produce two different action sequences, no simulation result means anything and no firing can be explained. It is also the property most easily broken by an innocuous change (a dict iteration, a wall-clock read, an unordered set), which is why it needs a permanent automated gate rather than a one-off verification.

## Scope / Deliverables
- **Determinism suite**: run a fixed set of recorded replay windows (from E26) through the engine N times (N>=3, and >=10 in the nightly run) with a corpus of armed-in-simulate rules, asserting byte-identical sequences of `RuleEvent` records, planned actions, timestamps and `skipped_reason` values.
  - Include windows chosen to be awkward: a dead market where `on_bar_close` fires with no trades, a burst where `on_price_update` fires thousands of times, a window containing a feed gap, and one spanning a UTC day boundary (for `once_per=day` and daily counters).
  - Assert cross-process determinism too — run in separate processes with different `PYTHONHASHSEED` values, which is how unordered-iteration bugs surface.
- **E2E suite (Playwright, web and Electron)** covering the rule-engine journeys this epic owns:
  1. Create a rule via the API, simulate it over a recorded window, read the coverage statement, arm it on demo, observe it fire, open its firing in SCR-087 and follow the link to the resulting order.
  2. The **editor-switch test for every construct in the metric/action vocabulary** required by US-RULE-006's NFR — driven through the real UI, asserting the round-trip indicator state and that the IR hash is unchanged.
  3. Attempt to arm without a simulation, with an open safety warning, and on an account without permission — each refused with its specific reason.
  4. Two conflicting rules: detection at arm time, precedence set through SCR-086, arbitration observed in the firing log with one action superseded.
  5. Export a rule, re-import it, assert no account ids or armed state in the bundle and that the import lands disarmed.
  6. Inspect a rule's canonical IR in SCR-088 and confirm the round-trip diff is empty.
- **Contract test suite** for all thirteen `/rules*` operations and the `rules` WS topic, replaying every documented example from `22-api-openapi.yaml`.
- Wiring into CI with the determinism suite as a **required check** on PRs touching the evaluator.

## Out of scope
- The compiler-level round-trip property suite — **E35-Q02** (this ticket covers the UI-level switch test).
- Load and performance measurement — **E35-Q04**; chaos — **E35-Q05**.
- E2E for the editors' own authoring interactions — E36/E37 own those; this ticket covers the switch and the IR equivalence.

## Acceptance criteria
```gherkin
Scenario: The same window always produces the same actions
  Given a recorded replay window and a corpus of simulate-mode rules
  When the window is replayed ten times across separate processes with differing hash seeds
  Then the sequence of rule events, planned actions and skip reasons is identical in every run

Scenario: A dead market still fires scheduled rules (edge case)
  Given a replay window with no trades for several bar intervals
  When an on_bar_close rule is evaluated
  Then it fires on schedule in every run, because a bar closes on the clock even with no trade

Scenario: Every vocabulary construct survives an editor switch
  Given one rule per construct in the metric and action vocabulary
  When each is opened in the other editor and returned through the real UI
  Then the round-trip indicator reports identical and the IR hash is unchanged

Scenario: Arming preconditions are enforced through the UI and the API (failure case)
  Given a rule with no completed simulation on its current version
  When arming is attempted through the dialog and then by a crafted API call
  Then both are refused with the same reason and no mode change occurs

Scenario: A non-deterministic regression is caught (failure case)
  Given a deliberately introduced unordered iteration in the evaluator
  When the determinism suite runs
  Then it fails and names the first divergent event
```

## Technical notes / design
Determinism assertions compare a normalised event stream: strip wall-clock fields that are legitimately variable (`duration_ms`, absolute `started_at`) and compare everything that is supposed to be a function of the input — event order, `node_ref`, condition results, metric values, planned actions, `skipped_reason`. Be explicit about which fields are excluded and why, in a comment, because a lenient comparison quietly stops testing anything.

The `PYTHONHASHSEED` variation is the highest-value trick here: most non-determinism in Python engines comes from iterating a set or a dict built from unordered input, and it is invisible in a single-process run.

The Electron E2E run covers the same journeys as the web run; per `03-testing-strategy.md` both targets are required for R3. Keep the journey definitions shared and the drivers thin so the two do not diverge.

E2E tests run against staging (demo) with seeded accounts and recorded fixtures, never against live — and the suite must assert, via a network spy, that no request reached a live endpoint during a simulation-mode journey.

## Test plan
This is test code. Its own guard is the fifth acceptance scenario (a deliberately introduced non-determinism must fail the suite). Runtime budgets: determinism suite under 6 minutes in PR CI (3 repeats) and unbounded nightly (10 repeats); E2E suite under 15 minutes.

## Security notes
Journey 3 and journey 5 are security journeys: arming-precondition bypass and export content. They must run in CI as ordinary tests rather than being treated as a security-team activity, because a control that is only checked during a security review regresses between reviews. No real credentials appear in any fixture; demo accounts are seeded with test keys held in the CI secret store.

## Accessibility notes
The E2E suite includes a keyboard-only variant of the arming journey (journey 1) since SCR-085's keyboard path is a named requirement; the comprehensive a11y audit is E35-Q06.

## Performance notes
Not a performance suite, but it must not become the slowest gate on the queue: budgets above are enforced, and the nightly deep run carries the expensive repetitions.

## Observability
On failure the determinism suite emits the first divergent event with its full context, and the E2E suite captures traces, screenshots and the server logs for the window — a failing E2E without an artefact is a flake report, not a bug report.

## Definition of Done
- [ ] Test artefacts committed to the repository (plan document, suites, fixtures, scripts) and runnable by any engineer from a documented command.
- [ ] Results recorded on the ticket with pass/fail per scenario and links to CI runs.
- [ ] Any defect found is filed as a Bug with reproduction steps, expected vs actual, severity, and the test layer that should have caught it earlier.
- [ ] New automated suites wired into CI with their runtime budget agreed, and marked required where the roadmap's quality gates demand it.
- [ ] Reviewed by the second QA/SDET and by the rule-engine backend lead.
- [ ] Sign-off comment posted; no P0/P1 defects open against the covered scope.
- [ ] The determinism suite is a **required check** for PRs touching the evaluator package; the E2E suite runs on the merge queue and nightly.

## Dependencies

title: Build the rule-engine performance and load benchmarks
body:
## Context
The rule engine sits on the hot path twice: as an always-on evaluator reacting to the same tick stream that drives the charts, and as a synchronous `pre_trade_check` veto inside the order submission path, which is governed by budget #4 (order submit → ack p95 <300 ms, a hard R3 gate).

The published budgets this ticket must measure are scattered across the specification: evaluation within `limits.evaluation_timeout_ms` (250 ms default); `POST /rules/validate` <=300 ms; compile + round-trip diff <=500 ms p95 for a 100-node rule; conflict detection <=1 s for 500 rules; a 14-day single-symbol simulation <=60 s; SCR-087 10k rows within 8 ms scripting per frame. Without an automated benchmark each of these is an aspiration.

## Scope / Deliverables
- **Evaluator benchmark**: N armed rules (N in 10, 50, 200, 500) over a recorded high-activity window, measuring evaluation latency p50/p95/p99 per trigger type, total CPU, and the metric-memoisation hit rate (ten rules referencing `atr(14)` must cost one computation — assert it, do not assume it).
- **`pre_trade_check` micro-benchmark**: latency distribution of the synchronous veto path, asserting it consumes a negligible share of the 300 ms submit→ack budget and that its own 25 ms budget holds at the 99th percentile with the built-in `sys.*` pre-trade rules enabled.
- **API benchmarks** (k6): `/rules/validate` and `/rules/{id}/compile` at a 100-node document against their 300 ms and 500 ms p95 budgets; `GET /rules` paging a 500-rule dataset; `GET /rules/{id}/runs` paging a 100k-run history.
- **Conflict-detection benchmark** over a seeded 500-rule dataset against the 1 s budget.
- **Simulation benchmark**: 14 days of one symbol at 1-minute granularity against the 60 s budget, including the streamed-partial-results behaviour.
- **Log write-path benchmark**: sustained matched-run write throughput, asserting logging adds <=1 ms to an evaluation at p99 and that the queue's back-pressure drop order is respected under saturation.
- **Frontend budget check**: SCR-087 with a 10k-row fixture measured against the 8 ms scripting-per-frame budget.
- CI wiring with recorded baselines and a regression threshold that fails the build on a breach, so a regression surfaces same-day rather than at the R3 gate.

## Out of scope
- Chaos and failure-injection — **E35-Q05**.
- Optimisation work itself — that is filed as Tasks against the owning story if a budget is breached.
- The platform-wide load profile (WS fan-out, ingestion soak) — the performance epic and E05/E08 own those; this ticket measures the rule engine's share.

## Acceptance criteria
```gherkin
Scenario: Every published budget is measured
  Given the budgets for evaluation, validate, compile, conflict detection, simulation and the fire-history table
  When the benchmark suite runs
  Then each produces a recorded number compared against its budget with a pass or fail

Scenario: Memoisation is proven, not assumed
  Given ten armed rules each referencing atr(14) on the same symbol and timeframe
  When a trigger fires for all ten
  Then the metric is computed once and the cache-hit counter confirms it

Scenario: The pre-trade veto does not endanger the submit budget (failure case)
  Given the built-in pre-trade rules enabled
  When order submission is benchmarked
  Then the rule-engine contribution stays within its 25 ms budget at p99 and the end-to-end submit to ack p95 remains under 300 ms

Scenario: A regression fails the build (failure case)
  Given a change that increases p99 evaluation latency beyond the agreed threshold over baseline
  When CI runs the benchmark
  Then the build fails naming the regressed metric, its baseline and its new value

Scenario: Logging degrades gracefully under saturation (edge case)
  Given the log write queue saturated
  When the benchmark applies sustained load
  Then non-matched simulate records are dropped first, matched runs and errors are never dropped, and the drop counter increments
```

## Technical notes / design
Benchmarks run on a pinned runner profile so numbers are comparable run to run; a benchmark on variable hardware measures the hardware. Record the profile alongside the results.

Use recorded replay windows rather than synthetic tick generators for the evaluator benchmark — synthetic uniform ticks understate the cost of the bursty real distribution, which is exactly where the timeout risk lives.

For the 500-rule case, scope the rules across multiple symbols and accounts so per-scope-instance expansion is exercised: 500 rules over 10 symbols is 5 000 instances, which is the number that actually matters.

Regression thresholds should be generous enough not to flake (suggest 15% over baseline on p99) but tight enough to catch a real regression; agree the number with the Architect and record it in `06-performance-and-load-standard.md`.

## Test plan
This is measurement code. Its guard is a self-check that the harness detects a deliberately inserted 50 ms sleep in the evaluation path.

## Security notes
Benchmarks run against staging (demo) with seeded data and no real credentials. One security-relevant finding class to watch for: if the evaluator's cost scales badly with rule count, a user could create many rules as an accidental denial of service — if the numbers suggest that, file it against the STRIDE model in E35-X01 rather than only as a performance note.

## Accessibility notes
N/A — measurement infrastructure, except that the SCR-087 frontend budget check protects the usability of the log for everyone, including assistive-technology users whose stack is more sensitive to heavy DOM work.

## Performance notes
This ticket *is* the performance deliverable. Budgets restated: evaluation within 250 ms default timeout; `pre_trade_check` within 25 ms p99; validate <=300 ms; compile+diff <=500 ms p95 at 100 nodes; conflict detection <=1 s at 500 rules; simulation <=60 s for 14 days of one symbol; log write <=1 ms added at p99; SCR-087 <=8 ms scripting per frame at 10k rows.

## Observability
Results are published to the CI performance dashboard with the run's commit and runner profile, and the measured numbers are folded into `docs/plan/06-performance-and-load-standard.md` and E35-T06's documentation reconciliation so future work compares against reality.

## Definition of Done
- [ ] Test artefacts committed to the repository (plan document, suites, fixtures, scripts) and runnable by any engineer from a documented command.
- [ ] Results recorded on the ticket with pass/fail per scenario and links to CI runs.
- [ ] Any defect found is filed as a Bug with reproduction steps, expected vs actual, severity, and the test layer that should have caught it earlier.

title: Run chaos scenarios against the rule engine
body:
## Context
The R3 chaos quality gate requires "WS kill mid-order, backend restart mid-TWAP, Postgres failover mid-fan-out — all resume to a correct, reconciled state". The rule engine has its own versions of each, and its failure modes are more insidious than the OMS's because a rule acts *without a human watching*: an engine that silently stops evaluating looks identical to an engine whose rules simply have not matched.

The specification already states the intended behaviour under failure, so this ticket verifies rather than discovers: §11.5 E10 (reconnect does not replay missed triggers; re-evaluate current state once; dedupe prevents duplicates), §11.7's disconnect guard (armed rules are **paused** while the private WS is disconnected or reconciliation is running; the native SL keeps protecting positions; the UI shows "rules paused — feed degraded"), and §11.5 E9 (a failed action stops the remaining actions; nothing is rolled back; the partial outcome is alerted).

## Scope / Deliverables
Chaos scenarios, each run against staging (demo) with fault injection and each asserting a **specific** recovery state rather than "it did not crash":
1. **Private WS disconnect while rules are armed** — armed rules pause within the guard's window, no action is taken on stale state, the UI degraded state is published, and on reconnect state is re-evaluated exactly once with no replay of missed triggers.
2. **Backend restart mid-fire**, between two actions of a multi-action rule — the completed action is recorded, the remaining actions are not silently resumed, the partial outcome is alerted, and the dedupe key prevents the first action re-executing.
3. **Backend restart during a pending `require_confirmation` fire** — the fire expires rather than resurrecting, because the market state that justified it is gone.
4. **Postgres unavailable while the log queue fills** — evaluation continues, the drop order is respected (non-matched simulate records first), matched runs and errors survive, and the drop counter increments; on recovery the queue drains without duplicating rows.
5. **Exchange 5xx and rate-limit `10018` on a rule action** — the action fails with the correct classification, `on_error` semantics apply, and the rule's consecutive-error counter advances toward auto-disable rather than retrying indefinitely.
6. **Clock skew injected** — `sys.clock_drift_block` vetoes order entry, and rules depending on time windows behave per specification rather than firing spuriously.
7. **Feed goes stale without disconnecting** (data stops but the socket stays open) — the stale-data guard skips evaluations with `stale_data`, which is the harder and more realistic variant of scenario 1.
8. **Auto-disable path** — force `kill_switch_on_error_count` consecutive errors and assert the rule disables itself, emits a critical alert, and requires human re-arm rather than self-recovering.
Each scenario is scripted, repeatable and wired into the nightly chaos run, with its expected recovery state asserted programmatically.

## Out of scope
- OMS-side chaos (order reconciliation, fan-out failover) — **E29**/**E34**/**E45** own those; this ticket covers the rule engine's behaviour when they fail underneath it.
- Kill-switch drills — **E39**.
- Performance under load — **E35-Q04**.

## Acceptance criteria
```gherkin
Scenario: Rules pause rather than act on stale state
  Given armed rules and a private WS disconnect
  When the disconnect exceeds the guard threshold
  Then armed rules are paused, no action is taken, the degraded state is published to the UI
  And native exchange-side stops remain in force and untouched

Scenario: Reconnect does not replay history
  Given thirty seconds of missed triggers during a disconnect
  When the connection is restored
  Then missed triggers are counted but not replayed, current state is re-evaluated exactly once, and no duplicate action occurs

Scenario: A restart mid-fire leaves an honest partial state (failure case)
  Given a three-action fire interrupted by a backend restart after the first action
  When the backend returns
  Then the completed action is recorded, the remaining actions are not silently executed, the partial outcome is alerted
  And replaying the fire cannot duplicate the completed action

Scenario: A silently stale feed is detected (edge case)
  Given a connected socket delivering no data
  When evaluations are triggered
  Then each is skipped with stale_data, the skip counter increments, and no action is taken on the frozen values

Scenario: Repeated errors disable the rule rather than looping (failure case)
  Given consecutive action errors reaching kill_switch_on_error_count
  When the threshold is reached
  Then the rule auto-disables, a critical alert fires, and it stays disabled until a human re-arms it
```

## Technical notes / design
Fault injection via a proxy in front of the exchange WS/REST (to drop, delay, freeze or return 5xx/`10018`), container control for backend restarts, and a Postgres pause for the storage scenarios. Scenario 7 — a live socket delivering nothing — is the one most often missed by chaos suites because it requires the proxy to hold the connection open while suppressing frames; it is also the closest to real-world exchange behaviour under stress.

Each scenario asserts three things: the immediate behaviour, the recovery state, and the **observability** — the right metric incremented and the right log or alert emitted. An engine that behaves correctly but silently is a half pass, because an operator cannot tell a paused engine from a quiet market.

Run against staging (demo) with seeded positions carrying native stops, so scenario 1's assertion that native stops remain in force is meaningful rather than vacuous.

## Test plan
This ticket is test execution and automation. Scenarios are scripted for the nightly chaos run; each produces an artefact bundle (logs, metrics, timeline) so a failure is diagnosable without re-running.

## Security notes
Chaos testing is a security activity as much as a reliability one: several scenarios probe whether a degraded system fails **safe**. Scenario 1's assertion that native stops remain in force is the safety invariant under failure (ADR-0008), and scenario 8's auto-disable prevents a malfunctioning rule from acting repeatedly. Findings feed the STRIDE model in E35-X01. All testing is against demo; no live path is exercised.

## Accessibility notes
One assertion belongs here: the degraded state must reach the UI as text ("rules paused — feed degraded"), not only as a colour change or an icon, so a screen-reader user learns that automation has stopped. Verified in coordination with E35-Q06.

## Performance notes
Scenario 4 overlaps with the log write-path benchmark in E35-Q04; run it here under failure rather than under load, and cross-reference the results rather than duplicating the harness.

## Observability
Every scenario asserts its observability signature: `rule_skipped_total{reason}`, `rule_missed_triggers_total`, `rule_auto_disarmed_total`, `rule_log_dropped_total`, the paused-state publication on the `rules`/`system` topics, and the critical alert on auto-disable. A scenario that passes behaviourally but emits no signal is recorded as a partial pass with a follow-up ticket.

## Definition of Done
- [ ] Test artefacts committed to the repository (plan document, suites, fixtures, scripts) and runnable by any engineer from a documented command.
- [ ] Results recorded on the ticket with pass/fail per scenario and links to CI runs.
- [ ] Any defect found is filed as a Bug with reproduction steps, expected vs actual, severity, and the test layer that should have caught it earlier.
- [ ] New automated suites wired into CI with their runtime budget agreed, and marked required where the roadmap's quality gates demand it.
- [ ] Reviewed by the second QA/SDET and by the rule-engine backend lead.
- [ ] Sign-off comment posted; no P0/P1 defects open against the covered scope.
- [ ] All eight scenarios scripted, repeatable, and wired into the nightly chaos run with artefact capture.

## Dependencies
Blocked by **E35-Q03**. Exercises failure paths owned by **E29** (private WS, reconciliation), **E39** (kill-switch interaction) and the storage tier. Feeds **E35-Q07** and the R3 chaos quality gate.

## Branch

## References

- `docs/plan/27-adrs/ADR-0007-rule-ir.md` — one canonical IR, binding rules 1-8

title: Accessibility audit of the six rule-engine screens
body:
## Context
The R3 a11y quality gate requires "Order ticket, DOM ladder and both rule editors fully keyboard-operable; danger/confirm patterns announced". E35's screens are the rule engine's half of that: the arming dialog is a danger/confirm pattern, the fire history is a dense live-updating table, and the IR inspector presents a code document as primary content.

`02-definition-of-ready-done.md` §8 removes any internal-tool exemption, and the Epic DoD requires axe-core CI green plus at least one manual screen-reader pass for every new screen. E35-D04 specified the expected behaviour at design time; this ticket verifies the build against that specification.

## Scope / Deliverables
- **Automated**: axe-core in CI across SCR-084, SCR-085, SCR-086, SCR-087, SCR-088 and SCR-089 in **every enumerated state** (not just the default), wired so a new violation fails the build.
- **Manual screen-reader passes** with at least two combinations (NVDA + Firefox or Chrome on Windows, VoiceOver + Safari on macOS), covering:
  - the arming dialog: `role="alertdialog"`, the plain-language behaviour restatement read as the description, the DEMO-preselected radio group, the typed confirmation and 2FA fields' labels and hints, focus trap and restore
  - the fire history: table semantics, the nested condition-value table read comprehensibly, polite announcement of appended rows without focus movement or scroll disruption
  - the IR inspector: the described-by note on the read-only region and the keyboard-navigable structured tree alternative
  - the conflict resolver: each resolution announced with its consequence
  - the simulation panel: progress announced politely, results readable as a table, the timeline's text-list equivalent
- **Keyboard-only traversal** of every journey: create → simulate → arm → inspect a firing → resolve a conflict → export, with no pointer at any point.
- **Zoom and reflow** at 125% and 200% without clipping or horizontal scrolling of content.
- **Contrast verification** of the built UI in both themes against the ratios E35-D04 annotated.
- **Reduced-motion** verification: every animation has its alternative and no status is conveyed by motion alone.
- Findings filed as Bugs with `priority/*`, each naming the WCAG 2.2 criterion and the E35-D04 specification item it violates.

## Out of scope
- The node-graph editor's canvas accessibility — **E37**, which carries the substantial keyboard-alternative work.
- Design-time review — **E35-D04**, already done; this is the built-screen audit.
- Visual design QA — **E35-D06**.

## Acceptance criteria
```gherkin
Scenario: Automated checks cover every state
  Given the enumerated states of all six screens
  When axe-core runs in CI
  Then every state is asserted and the build fails on any new violation

Scenario: A rule can be armed without a pointer
  Given a keyboard-only user
  When they simulate a rule and arm it on demo
  Then every step is reachable and operable, focus is visible throughout, and Escape cancels the dialog without arming

Scenario: A firing is comprehensible through a screen reader
  Given a fired rule in the history
  When a screen-reader user navigates to it
  Then they can determine the trigger, the condition values and the resulting actions from the announced content alone

Scenario: The live log does not disrupt reading (edge case)
  Given a screen-reader user reading a history row while new firings arrive
  When rows append
  Then announcements are polite and batched, focus does not move, and the reading position is preserved

Scenario: The IR document is navigable without sight (failure case)
  Given a 100 KB canonical IR in the inspector
  When a screen-reader user opens it
  Then the structured tree alternative is available and navigable by keyboard, rather than only an unnavigable pre-formatted block
```

## Technical notes / design
Automated coverage of *every state* is the part usually skipped, and it matters here because the error, partial and blocked states carry the most important copy. Drive the states from the same fixtures the component tests use so the audit cannot silently cover fewer states than exist.

For the manual passes, script the journeys in advance and record the sessions, so a finding can be replayed rather than argued about. Test with the screen reader's default verbosity rather than a tuned configuration — the default is what a real user meets.

Batching of live-region announcements (scenario 4) is a specification item from E35-D04; verify the implemented batching interval rather than merely checking that a live region exists.

## Test plan
This ticket is the audit. Its artefacts are the axe-core CI configuration, the recorded manual sessions, the findings log and the filed Bugs.

## Security notes
One overlap: the arming dialog is both a danger pattern and a security control. An a11y fix that shortens or removes the plain-language behaviour restatement would weaken the safety confirmation — any such fix must be reviewed against the security intent, not applied as a pure a11y change.

## Accessibility notes
This ticket *is* the a11y deliverable, verified against `docs/plan/05-accessibility-standard.md` (WCAG 2.2 AA) and the E35-D04 specification. Standards applied include the 2.2-specific focus-appearance and dragging-alternative criteria.

## Performance notes
The live-region batching requirement is also a performance requirement: announcing every appended row at a high append rate saturates the screen reader and degrades the whole session. Verify the batching interval under a high-firing-rate fixture.

## Observability
Findings are logged with the screen, state, WCAG criterion and specification item, so recurring classes of failure (for example, colour-only status) are visible across the product rather than fixed one screen at a time.

## Definition of Done
- [ ] Test artefacts committed to the repository (plan document, suites, fixtures, scripts) and runnable by any engineer from a documented command.
- [ ] Results recorded on the ticket with pass/fail per scenario and links to CI runs.
- [ ] Any defect found is filed as a Bug with reproduction steps, expected vs actual, severity, and the test layer that should have caught it earlier.
- [ ] New automated suites wired into CI with their runtime budget agreed, and marked required where the roadmap's quality gates demand it.
- [ ] Reviewed by the second QA/SDET and by the rule-engine backend lead.
- [ ] Sign-off comment posted; no P0/P1 defects open against the covered scope.
- [ ] axe-core wired into CI across all six screens in every enumerated state, failing the build on new violations.
- [ ] At least two screen-reader/browser combinations exercised, sessions recorded.
- [ ] All findings filed with WCAG criterion references; no P0/P1 a11y defects open.

## Dependencies

title: Execute the exploratory charters, regression pack and epic QA sign-off
body:
## Context
The Epic DoD requires "an Epic-level regression/exploratory pass executed and recorded, not just child-ticket QA", and every Story DoD requires a QA sign-off comment with pass/fail per scenario. This ticket closes both for E35.

It is deliberately the last QA ticket in the epic and deliberately human: the automated suites (Q02-Q05) verify the properties we thought to specify, and the exploratory charters from E35-Q01 exist to find the ones we did not. For a subsystem that places orders without a human watching, that gap is the part worth paying for.

## Scope / Deliverables
- Execute the **six exploratory charters** defined in E35-Q01, 90 minutes each, session-based, each with a written debrief covering what was tested, what was found, what obstacles arose and what should be tested next:
  1. Make an armed rule act on an account you were never granted.
  2. Make the form and graph representations of one rule disagree.
  3. Make a simulation result misleading enough to justify arming a rule you should not.
  4. Make the engine act on stale or missing data.
  5. Lose a firing from the log, or make the log say something the engine did not do.
  6. Arm a rule without meeting the arming preconditions, by any path including crafted API calls.
- Execute the **full black-box test plan** from E35-Q01 across all nine user stories, recording pass/fail per scenario.
- Execute the **regression pack** against the R3 release candidate.
- **Cross-epic interaction checks** that no single ticket owns: a rule action fanning out through E34 to five accounts each with its native SL; a rule action blocked by E39's risk caps and by the kill-switch; a rule-originated trade appearing correctly in E41's journal with `origin_rule_id` set; an alert sharing the IR grammar (E40) behaving consistently with a rule using the same conditions.
- **Verify R3 exit criteria 5 and 6** end to end and record the evidence on the epic ticket, since the epic's DoD names them.
- Consolidate every open defect against E35 scope, confirm zero P0/P1 remain, and post the **epic QA sign-off**.

## Out of scope
- Building automation — Q02-Q05 own that; defects found here that warrant automation are filed as Tasks against the appropriate suite.
- The a11y audit — **E35-Q06**, already complete; its findings are consolidated here.
- The security review and sign-off — **E35-X03**, which runs in parallel and is consolidated alongside.

## Acceptance criteria
```gherkin
Scenario: Every charter is executed with a debrief
  Given the six exploratory charters
  When the sessions complete
  Then each has a written debrief and every finding is filed as a Bug with reproduction steps and the test layer that should have caught it

Scenario: The full plan is executed and recorded
  Given the black-box test plan across the nine user stories
  When execution completes
  Then every scenario has a recorded pass or fail, and every failure has a filed Bug

Scenario: Cross-epic behaviour is verified (edge case)
  Given a rule action that fans out to five accounts
  When it fires on demo
  Then each leg is sized by its own account profile, carries a native exchange-side stop, and the resulting trade group records origin_rule_id and
       origin_rule_run_id, with the trade appearing in the journal attributed to the rule

Scenario: Exit criteria are proven, not assumed
  Given R3 exit criteria 5 and 6
  When the verification runs
  Then the thirty-rule corpus round-trips with identical hashes and the replay determinism holds, with both results recorded on the epic ticket

Scenario: Sign-off is conditional on a clean board (failure case)
  Given an open P0 or P1 defect against E35 scope
  When sign-off is attempted
  Then it is withheld until the defect is resolved or explicitly accepted by the Owner with a recorded rationale
```

## Technical notes / design
Run against the R3 release candidate on staging (demo), with a seeded environment reaching every designed state — the seeding plan from E35-Q01 is a prerequisite, and any state that cannot be reached is itself a finding.

For charter 6 in particular, use a raw HTTP client rather than the UI: the whole point is that the server enforces the preconditions, and a UI-only test cannot establish that. Coordinate with E35-X02 so the two activities complement rather than duplicate.

Charter 5 deserves extra time. "The log says something the engine did not do" is the hardest class of defect to find and the most damaging, because every later investigation trusts the log. Cross-check a sample of firings against the OMS's own order records and the audit trail.

## Test plan
This ticket is test execution. Every finding is filed with reproduction steps, expected vs actual, severity, and the test layer that should have caught it — that last field is what turns an exploratory finding into a durable automated test.

## Security notes
Charters 1 and 6 are abuse-case testing; their findings feed **E35-X01**'s STRIDE model and are reviewed with the Security engineer before sign-off. The cross-epic native-SL check contributes evidence to R3 exit criterion 2 (no path opens a position without a native exchange-side stop), which is a required safety gate rather than a QA nicety. All execution is against demo.

## Accessibility notes
E35-Q06's findings are consolidated here; the sign-off states the a11y status explicitly, and any open a11y defect is listed with its priority rather than being folded silently into a pass.

## Performance notes
E35-Q04's measured numbers are consolidated into the sign-off so the epic's performance position against the R3 budgets is stated in one place, including any accepted deviation.

## Observability
The sign-off records which audit events were observed in practice for each audited action — an audited action with no observed audit row is a P1 defect, since the audit trail is the epic's non-repudiation control.

## Definition of Done
- [ ] Test artefacts committed to the repository (plan document, suites, fixtures, scripts) and runnable by any engineer from a documented command.
- [ ] Results recorded on the ticket with pass/fail per scenario and links to CI runs.
- [ ] Any defect found is filed as a Bug with reproduction steps, expected vs actual, severity, and the test layer that should have caught it earlier.
- [ ] New automated suites wired into CI with their runtime budget agreed, and marked required where the roadmap's quality gates demand it.
- [ ] Reviewed by the second QA/SDET and by the rule-engine backend lead.
- [ ] Sign-off comment posted; no P0/P1 defects open against the covered scope.
- [ ] All six charters executed with written debriefs.
- [ ] Full black-box plan executed with pass/fail per scenario.
- [ ] Regression pack executed against the R3 release candidate.
- [ ] R3 exit criteria 5 and 6 verified and the evidence recorded on the E35 epic ticket.
- [ ] Zero P0/P1 defects open against E35 scope, or explicit Owner acceptance recorded.
- [ ] Epic QA sign-off comment posted, consolidating the a11y (Q06), performance (Q04), chaos (Q05) and security (X03) positions.

## Dependencies
Blocked by **E35-Q05** and **E35-Q06** (the last automated and a11y work). Runs alongside **E35-X03**. Its sign-off is a precondition for the E35 epic DoD and feeds the R3 PRR.

title: Store, version and mode-switch rules through the rules API
body:
## Context
> **Re-scoped 2026-09-24 for full xstate-statemachine adoption (ADR-0016 Accepted):** Ticket becomes a direct `B9` (`rule_instance`) lifecycle implementer on `xstate-statemachine`. The mode switch (armed/simulate/disarmed) is the `B9` chart itself.

US-RULE-001 requires rules to be versioned with an auditable history and migrated safely on load; ADR-0007 binding rule 5 makes rules immutable once saved, so editing creates a new version and audit records reference `(rule_id, version)` "so a firing can always be explained against the exact logic that ran".

The mode transition is the most safety-critical operation in the epic. `22-api-openapi.yaml` states arming requires: a validated active version with zero errors, **at least one completed simulation run on that exact `ir_hash`**, no open validation warnings of class `safety`, and `orders:write` on every bound account when the rule sends orders. `21-database-schema.md` §3.4.1 adds that arming is a dangerous permission (`rules.arm.live`) requiring fresh step-up MFA, and that the transition writes an audit entry carrying the IR hash so "what exactly was armed" is provable.

An armed rule also keeps executing its previously active version until a new version is **explicitly** activated via `PUT /rules/{id}/active-version` — a save must never mutate what is running underneath the runtime (US-RULE-006 "switch while armed").

## Scope / Deliverables
- `GET /api/v1/rules` (cursor paginated, filters `mode` and `scope`, account-scoped by grants), `POST /api/v1/rules` (always stores version 1 in `mode: disabled`), `GET/PUT/DELETE /api/v1/rules/{ruleId}`.
- `PUT /api/v1/rules/{ruleId}` creating an immutable new `rule_versions` row (`version = previous + 1`) with its `ir_hash` and `compiler_version`, and **not** changing what an armed rule executes.
- `GET /api/v1/rules/{ruleId}/versions`, `GET /api/v1/rules/{ruleId}/versions/{versionId}` (full IR), `PUT /api/v1/rules/{ruleId}/active-version` (activate or roll back, with a note).
- `PUT /api/v1/rules/{ruleId}/mode` implementing every arming precondition above, idempotency-key required, audited and broadcast on the `rules` WS topic.
- **Optimistic concurrency** on save: a client saving over a version it did not see is rejected with a conflict naming the other editor and session, offering reload-and-reapply — silent last-writer-wins is never permitted (US-RULE-006 "concurrent edit in two tabs").
- Delete refused with `409 conflict` while the rule is `armed`; versions and run history retained for audit.
- The dedupe behaviour: a save producing an unchanged canonical IR returns the existing version rather than creating a duplicate (`UNIQUE (rule_id, ir_hash)`).
- Quarantine on load: a stored IR failing schema validation loads read-only, is force-disarmed, names the failing JSON path, and offers export-as-JSON — never partially executed (US-RULE-001 "Schema violation on load").
- Audit events `rule.created|updated|armed|disarmed|deleted`.
- Implement the `B9` lifecycle as `statechart/machines/B9.rule_instance.machine.json` (committed by E50-S01/S02, hash-locked). Do not hand-write the state enum or transition table.
- Build it only through `statechart.factory.build('rule_instance', lane=…)`, and restore it only through `statechart.persistence.restore`.
- Write guards, actions and services in `statechart/bindings/b09_rule_instance.py` as a `MachineLogic`. Everything is `async def`, and services are idempotent under re-entry.
- Add `tests/xstate_contract/test_b09_rule_instance.py`, which becomes a member of the blocking gate.
- All sends go through `statechart.gateway`.


## Out of scope
- Import/export of rule bundles (SCR-089) — **E35-S09**.
- The rules list UI (SCR-080) — E36.
- IR version upcasters — **E35-T05** (this story calls the migration hook; the upcasters themselves are T05).
- Simulation runs — **E35-S05** (this story enforces that one exists before arming).
- The arming *dialog* (SCR-085) — **E35-S08**.

## Acceptance criteria
```gherkin
Scenario: Every save is a new immutable version
  Given an existing rule at version 3
  When a semantically changed IR is saved
  Then version 4 is created with its own ir_hash and compiler_version, version 3 is unchanged
  And an armed rule continues executing version 3 until active-version is explicitly changed

Scenario: Arming requires proof the rule was simulated
  Given a rule whose active version has never completed a simulation on its exact ir_hash
  When PUT /api/v1/rules/{ruleId}/mode is called with mode armed
  Then the request is refused with 422 explaining the missing precondition
  And the rule stays in its previous mode

Scenario: Arming live needs step-up and is provably audited
  Given a rule scoped to environments including live and a user holding rules.arm.live
  When the rule is armed with a fresh step-up MFA token
  Then the transition succeeds, an audit entry is written containing the ir_hash, environment and scope
  And the new state is broadcast on the rules WS topic before the call returns

Scenario: Concurrent edits never silently overwrite (failure case)
  Given the same rule open in two sessions at version 5
  When the second session saves over a version the first did not see
  Then the save is rejected with an optimistic-concurrency conflict naming the other session
  And the client is offered reload-and-reapply

Scenario: Saving an unchanged rule creates nothing (edge case)
  Given a save whose canonical IR hashes to the active version's ir_hash
  When it is submitted
  Then no new version row is created and the existing version is returned

Scenario: A corrupt stored rule is quarantined (failure case)
  Given a rule_versions.ir document that fails schema validation
  When the rule is loaded
  Then it is returned read-only and force-disarmed, the failing JSON path is named, export-as-JSON is offered
  And the engine never evaluates it

Scenario: An armed rule cannot be deleted
  Given an armed rule
  When DELETE is called
  Then 409 conflict is returned instructing the caller to disarm first, and history is retained
```

## Technical notes / design
Mode-transition state machine: `disabled <-> simulate -> armed -> disabled`. Direct `disabled -> armed` is refused — §11.7's new-rule gate requires `min_simulation_fires` (default 5) or `min_simulation_hours` (default 24), whichever comes first, before `armed` is selectable, overridable only by the Owner with an audited reason. Implement the gate server-side; the UI merely reflects it.

Optimistic concurrency uses the version number as the token: the client sends `expected_version`; a mismatch returns `409` with the conflicting version, its author and session. Do not use `updated_at` timestamps — clock skew makes them unsafe.

`compiler_version` on every `rule_versions` row is the engine semver that validated the IR; it is what makes "this version was validated by an engine that no longer exists" detectable rather than mysterious.

Deletion is soft (`deleted_at`), consistent with `ux_rules_name` being partial on `deleted_at IS NULL`, so a name can be reused after deletion while history survives.

The `rules` WS broadcast on mode change must be emitted **before** the HTTP response returns (SCR-085: "the armed state is confirmed over `rules` before the dialog closes — never optimistically").
- Normative contract: `28-statechart-catalogue.md` §B9.1–.8. Mandatory config: 29-statechart-adoption-plan §1.2 (79-r14 §7 FINAL block). Hot-path parts listed in 29 §3 stay plain code.


## Test plan
Unit (>=90%): mode-transition matrix, every legal and illegal pair; arming precondition checks individually and in combination; optimistic-concurrency token handling; dedupe-on-identical-hash; soft delete and name reuse.
Contract: all nine `/rules*` CRUD/version/mode operations against `22-api-openapi.yaml`, including the documented `versions` example payload.
Integration (Postgres testcontainer): version chain across 10 saves; rollback to an earlier version; armed rule keeps executing v3 while v4 exists; quarantine path with a deliberately corrupted jsonb row.
Security/integration: arming without step-up, arming without `orders:write` on a bound account, arming with an open safety warning, arming a rule with `flatten_all_positions` without the extra acknowledgement — all refused with the right code and audited.
E2E: covered by **E35-Q03**.
- pure-API unit tests of the binding module with a `SimulatedClock`
- contract-suite membership (`test_b09_rule_instance.py`), covering both spellings and every §B9.7 invariant
- a snapshot round-trip (persist→restore) at every quiescence point the ticket introduces, plus a refused restore on a hash or HMAC mismatch


## Security notes
Threat sources: `docs/plan/04-security-program.md` (STRIDE per epic) and the E35 model produced by E35-X01.
- **Tampering** — the stored IR decides what an armed rule does; every version carries `ir_hash` (sha256 of canonical JSON) and the arming audit record embeds it, so "what exactly was armed" is provable.
- **Elevation of privilege** — a rule must never act on an account its author cannot trade; scope is enforced at *runtime on every action*, not only at save time (US-RULE-007 NFR).
- **Denial of service** — a pathological IR must not stall the evaluator: node counts are bounded by the JSON Schema (max 32 boolean children, max 10 actions, max 8 arithmetic operands) and every evaluation is time-boxed by `limits.evaluation_timeout_ms`.
- **Repudiation** — `rule_events` is append-only via the `trg_re_append`/`forbid_mutation` trigger.
- **Code execution** — the IR is data, never code (ADR-0007 R1): no `eval`, no expression strings parsed at runtime, no user scripting. Any PR introducing dynamic evaluation is an automatic reject.
Data classification: rule IR is *internal*; `rule_runs.input_snapshot` can contain account equity and position data — *financial/confidential*, never logged at INFO in plaintext to shared sinks. Security review label required.

This story is the privileged surface of the epic. Controls that must each have a dedicated negative test: `rules.arm.live` permission plus **fresh** step-up MFA for arming to an environment including `live`; `orders:write` on every bound account for order-sending actions; account-scoped listing so a manager never sees rules bound to accounts they are not granted; idempotency-key requirement on the mode endpoint so a retried arm cannot double-fire side-effects; and the audit entry embedding `ir_hash`. Attempting arming through a crafted request that skips the UI must fail identically — the freeze and permission checks are enforced at the API boundary, not in the UI (US-RULE-014 NFR, applied here by analogy).

## Accessibility notes
N/A for this backend story, except that every refusal message must be written as user-facing prose (it is rendered verbatim in SCR-085's error states and read by a screen reader), stating what is missing and what the user should do next — e.g. "This rule has not completed a simulation on its current version. Run a simulation before arming."

## Performance notes
`GET /rules` is the data source for SCR-080's virtualised table over 500 rules — cursor pagination with `ix_rules_active`, p95 <=150 ms for a 100-row page. Mode change takes effect server-side within 1 s including the WS broadcast (SCR-085 performance note).

## Observability
Audit: `rule.created|updated|armed|disarmed|deleted` with actor, environment, scope and `ir_hash`; `rule.armed` is high severity. Metrics: `rule_mode_transitions_total{from,to,result}`, `rule_versions_created_total`, `rule_save_conflicts_total`, `rule_quarantined_total`. WS: `RuleUpdate` frames on the `rules` topic.

## Definition of Done
- [ ] All Gherkin acceptance criteria covered by a named automated test.
- [ ] Coverage: rule-engine package >=90% line (R3 local policy, roadmap §7.4), other backend >=85%, frontend >=80%; CI coverage gate green.
- [ ] Docs updated where behaviour diverged: `docs/plan/24-internal-schemas.md` §11, `docs/plan/22-api-openapi.yaml`, `docs/plan/23-ws-protocol.md` §15.6, `docs/plan/21-database-schema.md` §3.4; ADR-0007 amended if an IR semantic changed.
- [ ] SAST (CodeQL/Semgrep/Bandit) and SCA (pip-audit/npm audit) clean or triaged with accepted-risk sign-off.
- [ ] QA sign-off comment posted with pass/fail per scenario.
- [ ] PR(s) <=400 LOC diff, merged via merge queue with 2 approvals incl. 1 code-owner.
- [ ] Feature-flag state recorded (`rules_global_enabled`; `rules.graph_editor` where relevant).
- [ ] Demoed at Sprint Review against staging (demo), or marked non-demoable infra-adjacent with Architect concurrence.
- [ ] `machine_hash` committed in `machine_hashes.lock`; `tools/lint_statecharts.py` green; `tests/xstate_contract` green; no import of `xstate_statemachine` outside `statechart/`.


## Dependencies
Blocked by **E35-T02** (tables) and **E35-T04** (compile/validate, whose result gates saving and arming). Depends on **E09** for step-up MFA and permission evaluation and **E27** for the account grants used in scoping. Blocks **E35-S05** (simulation records against a version) and the editors' save path in E36/E37.

title: Build the deterministic evaluator with snapshotting, guards and timeouts
body:
## Context
> **Re-scoped 2026-09-24 for full xstate-statemachine adoption (ADR-0016 Accepted):** **Excluded from the statechart migration** (29-statechart-adoption-plan §3): the deterministic evaluator is a hot-path, per-tick component (BENCH-2: 381 ev/s measured vs a 2,000 ev/s need), so it stays plain code permanently. This ticket is recorded only to confirm the exclusion; no behavioural or estimate change.

This is module **M15**, the heart of the epic: the one evaluator both editors' output runs through. `docs/plan/24-internal-schemas.md` §11.5 specifies its semantics as twelve binding rules (E1-E12) and a pipeline diagram; this story implements them literally, because R3 exit criterion 6 requires that "the same recorded window produces the same action sequence across runs" and simulation parity (E35-S05) depends on the live and simulated paths being the *same* code with a different sink.

The rules that most often get implemented wrongly, and which therefore carry dedicated acceptance scenarios here: `None` is false and never coerces to 0 (E3); one immutable `MetricSnapshot` per evaluation so sibling conditions cannot see different market states (E2); short-circuit evaluation that still logs which children were **not** evaluated so the trace is never misleading (E4); stale data **skips** rather than acts (E7); and `crosses_above`/`crosses_below` are false on the first evaluation after warmup or restart, so a reconnect cannot manufacture a phantom cross (§11.6).

## Scope / Deliverables
- The evaluator package implementing the §11.5 pipeline: trigger -> debounce -> build `MetricSnapshot` -> freshness check -> limits check -> evaluate the condition DAG -> mode branch. This story stops at "decide what to do"; performing it is E35-S03.
- **Trigger subscription** for all 13 trigger types (§11.6): bus subscriptions for `on_price_update`, `on_bar_close`, `on_order_fill`, `on_position_open`, `on_position_close`, `on_position_update`, `on_metric_change`, `on_signal`, `on_book_update` (throttled to 10 Hz), `on_liquidation`, `pre_trade_check` (synchronous veto before any order submission); a monotonic scheduler for `on_timer` and `on_schedule` (5-field UTC cron). Trigger-driven, never polled (E1).
- `MetricSnapshot` construction reading every referenced metric **once** into an immutable structure, with cross-rule memoisation so ten rules referencing `atr(14)` cost one computation (§7.3).
- Condition evaluation for every node type: `Comparison` (all 15 operators), `BooleanNode` (`all_of`/`any_of`/`none_of`/`n_of`), `TemporalNode` (`sustained_for`/`occurred_within`/`count_within`/`stable_for`), `ArithmeticNode` (9 ops) with unit-aware arithmetic.
- **Per-scope instances** (E6): a symbol-scoped rule over 3 symbols is 3 independent instances with independent `once`/cooldown state, keyed as `"BTCUSDT@acct-3f2a"` per the `scope_instance` field.
- Limit guards before evaluation: `once`/`once_per`, `cooldown_ms`, `max_fires_per_hour`, `max_fires_per_day`.
- Stale-data guard (E7): any metric older than `max_data_age_ms` (default 5 000, or 3x the stream cadence, whichever is larger) skips with `skipped_reason="stale_data"`.
- Evaluation timeout (E8): exceeding `limits.evaluation_timeout_ms` aborts, counts as an error, and contributes to `kill_switch_on_error_count`, after which the rule auto-disables with a `critical` alert and requires human re-arm.
- **Reconnect replay safety** (E10): after a disconnect the engine does not replay missed triggers; it re-evaluates current state once, and `once`/dedupe keys prevent duplicates. Missed triggers are counted as a metric.
- **Disconnect guard** (§11.7): while the private WS is disconnected or reconciliation is running, armed rules are **paused**; the native SL keeps protecting positions and the UI is told "rules paused — feed degraded".
- `NodeTrace` production for every evaluated and skipped node (§11.9) — the substrate the firing log (E35-S06) persists.

## Out of scope
- Executing actions and their safety limits — **E35-S03**.
- Runtime scope enforcement on actions — **E35-S04**.
- Persisting the trace — **E35-S06** (this story produces it in memory).
- Conflict arbitration between rules — **E35-S07**.
- Computing the metrics themselves — E12/E18-E25.
- The simulate sink — **E35-S05**.

## Acceptance criteria
```gherkin
Scenario: One snapshot per evaluation
  Given a rule whose two sibling conditions both read last_price
  And the price changes between the two reads in wall-clock terms
  When the rule evaluates
  Then both conditions observe the identical value from the single immutable snapshot

Scenario: None is false, never zero
  Given a condition referencing a metric still in warmup, with no position, or on a stale feed
  When the rule evaluates
  Then the condition is false, skipped_reason records warmup or stale_data, nothing throws
  And a comparison such as metric < 1 does not become true by treating the missing value as 0

Scenario: Short-circuit still produces a complete trace
  Given an all_of node whose first child is false
  When evaluation short-circuits
  Then the remaining children are recorded with result null meaning not evaluated, so the trace cannot be misread as all children being false

Scenario: A frozen feed never triggers action (failure case)
  Given any metric in the snapshot older than max_data_age_ms
  When the trigger fires
  Then the evaluation is skipped with skipped_reason stale_data and counted, and no condition is evaluated

Scenario: No phantom crosses after a restart (edge case)
  Given a rule using crosses_above and an engine that has just restarted
  When the first evaluation after warmup occurs
  Then crosses_above is false regardless of the current value, because no previous snapshot exists

Scenario: A slow evaluation is aborted and counted (failure case)
  Given an evaluation exceeding limits.evaluation_timeout_ms
  When the deadline passes
  Then the evaluation is aborted, recorded as an error, and after kill_switch_on_error_count consecutive errors the rule auto-disables with a critical alert

Scenario: Reconnect does not replay history (edge case)
  Given the engine was disconnected for 30 seconds while triggers fired
  When it reconnects
  Then missed triggers are counted but not replayed, current state is re-evaluated exactly once, and once/dedupe keys prevent any duplicate fire

Scenario: Deterministic ordering
  Given the same MetricSnapshot presented twice
  When the same rule evaluates
  Then children are evaluated in array order and the outcome and trace are identical
```

## Technical notes / design
Single-threaded asyncio evaluation per rule instance, with the snapshot built by a synchronous read of memoised metric values so no `await` can interleave a market update mid-evaluation — this is the mechanical guarantee behind E2 and is easier to hold than a lock discipline.

Temporal nodes need bounded state: `sustained_for` keeps the timestamp the child first became true; `occurred_within`/`count_within` keep a ring buffer of event timestamps bounded by `window_ms` (max 86 400 000 per the schema, so cap allocation accordingly); `stable_for` keeps the last change timestamp. State is per `scope_instance` and per `node_id`, and is **dropped** when the active version changes — a new version's temporal windows must not inherit the old version's history, which would be unexplainable.

`pre_trade_check` is the one synchronous trigger: the OMS calls the engine inline before submission and blocks on the verdict, with a hard budget well under the order submit -> ack p95 <300 ms gate (budget #4). Give it its own, tighter timeout (default 25 ms) and fail **open or closed** per the built-in rule's declaration — `sys.stale_feed_block` and `sys.clock_drift_block` fail **closed** (veto) because their purpose is to stop trading.

Auto-disable path: `kill_switch_on_error_count` consecutive errors -> set `rules.mode = 'disabled'` with `disabled_reason`, emit a `critical` alert, require human re-arm (§11.7 per-rule health row). Consecutive, not cumulative — a successful evaluation resets the counter.
- Per-tick evaluation is plain code (BENCH-2: 381 ev/s vs 2,000 ev/s required); this is a permanent exclusion from the `xstate-statemachine` catalogue per 29-statechart-adoption-plan §3, not a temporary gap.


## Test plan
Unit (>=90% — this package is held to the 90% R3 rule-module policy):
- Operator table: every one of the 15 comparison operators across numeric, enum and boolean operands, including `between`/`outside` bounds, `tolerance` on float `eq`, and `in_set`/`not_in_set` on enums.
- Boolean nodes incl. `n_of` boundaries (n=1, n=len, n>len rejected earlier by validation).
- All four temporal ops across window boundaries, with clock injected.
- Arithmetic ops incl. division by zero (must produce None, not raise) and unit propagation.
- `None` propagation through arithmetic into comparisons.
- Trigger dispatch for all 13 types with a fake bus and a fake monotonic scheduler; cron parsing incl. DST-free UTC assumption.
- Per-scope-instance isolation of `once`/cooldown/temporal state.
- Timeout abort, error counting, auto-disable at the threshold, counter reset on success.
Integration: against recorded fixtures from E26 replay — the determinism suite (run the same window three times, assert identical trace) which is R3 exit criterion 6; extended by **E35-Q03**.
Chaos: WS disconnect mid-evaluation and reconnect (armed rules pause, no replay) — extended by **E35-Q05**.
Perf: benchmark 200 armed rules over a 1-hour recorded window, asserting p99 evaluation latency inside the 250 ms default budget and memoisation reducing metric computations — **E35-Q04**.

## Security notes
Threat sources: `docs/plan/04-security-program.md` (STRIDE per epic) and the E35 model produced by E35-X01.
- **Tampering** — the stored IR decides what an armed rule does; every version carries `ir_hash` (sha256 of canonical JSON) and the arming audit record embeds it, so "what exactly was armed" is provable.
- **Elevation of privilege** — a rule must never act on an account its author cannot trade; scope is enforced at *runtime on every action*, not only at save time (US-RULE-007 NFR).
- **Denial of service** — a pathological IR must not stall the evaluator: node counts are bounded by the JSON Schema (max 32 boolean children, max 10 actions, max 8 arithmetic operands) and every evaluation is time-boxed by `limits.evaluation_timeout_ms`.
- **Repudiation** — `rule_events` is append-only via the `trg_re_append`/`forbid_mutation` trigger.
- **Code execution** — the IR is data, never code (ADR-0007 R1): no `eval`, no expression strings parsed at runtime, no user scripting. Any PR introducing dynamic evaluation is an automatic reject.
Data classification: rule IR is *internal*; `rule_runs.input_snapshot` can contain account equity and position data — *financial/confidential*, never logged at INFO in plaintext to shared sinks. Security review label required.

Specific to this ticket: the evaluator is the DoS-sensitive component. Controls: hard per-evaluation timeout; bounded temporal-state allocation derived from `window_ms`; bounded node counts enforced upstream by the schema; a per-rule error budget that auto-disables rather than looping. The disconnect guard is a safety control, not an optimisation — acting on stale state is how an automated system compounds a bad situation; it must have an explicit test, not just documentation. No user code is ever executed (ADR-0007 R1); a Semgrep rule (E35-X02) enforces the absence of `eval`/`exec`/`compile` in this package.

## Accessibility notes
N/A — backend engine. It does produce `skipped_reason` and `NodeTrace` values that become user-facing text in SCR-087, so each reason code needs a plain-language mapping agreed with design in E35-D03.

## Performance notes
Budgets: evaluation within `limits.evaluation_timeout_ms` (250 ms default, hard abort); `pre_trade_check` within its own 25 ms budget so it consumes a negligible share of the order submit -> ack p95 <300 ms gate (`06-performance-and-load-standard.md` budget #4); `on_book_update` throttled to 10 Hz; metric memoisation must demonstrably collapse duplicate computations across rules. All measured by the E35-Q04 benchmark and tracked in CI so regressions surface same-day.

## Observability
`rule_evaluations_total{rule_id,trigger,outcome}`, `rule_eval_duration_seconds` histogram (per trigger type), `rule_skipped_total{reason}`, `rule_missed_triggers_total`, `rule_auto_disarmed_total`, `rule_metric_cache_hits_total`, `rule_pre_trade_check_duration_seconds`. Structured logs on skip and abort carry `rule_id`, `version`, `ir_hash`, `scope_instance`. A `critical` alert on auto-disable.

## Definition of Done
- [ ] All Gherkin acceptance criteria covered by a named automated test.
- [ ] Coverage: rule-engine package >=90% line (R3 local policy, roadmap §7.4), other backend >=85%, frontend >=80%; CI coverage gate green.

- [ ] SAST (CodeQL/Semgrep/Bandit) and SCA (pip-audit/npm audit) clean or triaged with accepted-risk sign-off.
- [ ] QA sign-off comment posted with pass/fail per scenario.
- [ ] PR(s) <=400 LOC diff, merged via merge queue with 2 approvals incl. 1 code-owner.
- [ ] Feature-flag state recorded (`rules_global_enabled`; `rules.graph_editor` where relevant).
- [ ] Demoed at Sprint Review against staging (demo), or marked non-demoable infra-adjacent with Architect concurrence.

## Dependencies
Blocked by **E35-T04** (it evaluates validated IR). Consumes the MetricRegistry and event bus (E12/E18-E25) and the position/order state from **E29**. Blocks **E35-S03**, **E35-S04**, **E35-S05**, **E35-S06**.

## Branch
